title: Chain of Command, Delegation, and Supervision

unit.title: Program Orientation, Professionalism, and Healthcare Roles

sections.learningObjectives:
- Describe the chain of command in a medical office.
- Explain the role of delegation and supervision for medical office assistants.
- Recognize when to follow an order and when to escalate.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Think of it like a family tree at work: it shows who is in charge of whom and who you go to when you have a question.

### Question 2

The assistant is like a helper on a team led by a doctor or nurse; the helper does tasks the leader directs.

### Question 3

It is like knowing exactly which teacher to ask for permission at school, so no one is confused about who is in charge.

### Question 4

On your first day, you check the classroom chart or ask the principal who your teacher is, rather than guessing.

### Question 5

The doctor is the team captain; the assistant is a valued teammate who follows the captain's directions.

### Question 6

A supervisor is like a coach who watches the game, gives directions, and helps players improve.

### Question 7

If two teachers tell you opposite things, you ask them to sort it out first instead of guessing or doing half of each.

### Question 8

You tell your teacher first, not the whole school or strangers, when there is a problem in class.

### Question 9

If you think a rule should change, you tell the teacher or principal, not the lunch vendor.

### Question 10

It is like fire drills: knowing who to tell and who is in charge helps everyone respond safely.

### Question 11

You only take hall-pass orders from your own teacher, not from a stranger who claims to be important.

### Question 12

You tell your teacher about a mistake, and the teacher tells the principal if needed - that is going up the chain correctly.

### Question 13

The people in charge of the office are the doctor and the manager, not outside companies.

### Question 14

A tiny school has fewer teachers between you and the principal than a huge school does.

### Question 15

If a grown-up tells you something that breaks the house rules, you ask 'are you sure?' before doing it.

### Question 16

Only the coach who knows the game can tell a player which play to run, not a fan in the stands.

### Question 17

It is easier when you have one main teacher to ask, not ten who might all say different things.

### Question 18

You read the classroom rules and ask the principal, instead of guessing from how tall people are.

### Question 19

Delegation is when the teacher asks a helper to pass out papers - the helper can do it, and the teacher still watches over the class.

### Question 20

If the teacher asks you to water the class plant, the teacher is still in charge of the classroom.

### Question 21

You ask someone to feed your pet only if they know how, not just because they have free time.

### Question 22

If asked to do something you have never learned, you say 'I don't know how yet - can you teach me?'

### Question 23

The leader hands tasks down to the helper, like a captain giving plays to the team.

### Question 24

Good directions are like a recipe: it tells you what to do, what it should look like, and who to ask for help.

### Question 25

If you ask a friend to watch your lunchbox, it is still your lunchbox if something goes wrong.

### Question 26

Stocking supplies is like a helper filling the classroom's pencil cups - a normal, safe helper job.

### Question 27

You let someone walk the dog only if they know how and you still check in.

### Question 28

You can only ask someone to do chores if a grown-up put you in charge - not just because you are friends.

### Question 29

A favor is a friendly ask; delegation is an official 'this is your job now' from someone in charge.

### Question 30

If you don't understand part of the recipe, you ask the cook before you start, not after.

### Question 31

It is like the five checks before handing off a job: the right job to the right person at the right time with clear steps and a coach watching.

### Question 32

The teacher plans the lesson while helpers sharpen pencils and hand out papers - everyone does their part.

### Question 33

A supervisor is like a coach who stays nearby, watches, and helps while the player works.

### Question 34

Direct supervision is like the coach standing right next to you, ready to help.

### Question 35

How closely a coach watches you depends on how tricky the skill is and how much you have practiced.

### Question 36

You learn to ride a bike with someone holding the seat first, not alone on day one.

### Question 37

Tasks that touch a person's health need a trained leader watching over them, like a lifeguard at the pool.

### Question 38

The helper can keep answering the classroom phone while the teacher steps next door, because no big decisions are being made.

### Question 39

The riskier and newer the job, the closer the coach has to stand.

### Question 40

A good leader checks that the job is safe, explains it, and then checks the result.

### Question 41

If the teacher is busy, you still hand in your homework and ask them to check it later.

### Question 42

The teacher is ultimately responsible for the class, even when a helper does a task.

### Question 43

Only a trained leader, like a doctor or nurse, can watch over health tasks.

### Question 44

Some jobs the coach can guide by walkie-talkie; others need the coach right there - you check which is which.

### Question 45

A good coach tells you what you did well and what to fix so you get better, not so you feel bad.

### Question 46

You get training wheels first, and they come off once you show you can balance.

### Question 47

Doing a risky job alone with no coach nearby is like swimming without a lifeguard - you say no and get help.

### Question 48

Only the doctor or nurse in charge can hand out health tasks, like only the coach calls the plays.

### Question 49

You take health instructions from the doctor or nurse, not from another helper like yourself.

### Question 50

Whether the coach can ask you to do something depends on the rules and your training, not how the coach feels.

### Question 51

If a friend asks you to do a trick you never learned, you say 'we need the coach for that.'

### Question 52

Only the person with the official leader badge can hand out the important jobs.

### Question 53

A nurse practitioner is a leader too; you check the rules and your own training, then help.

### Question 54

The power to hand out tasks comes from official rules and the leader's license, not from opinions or ads.

### Question 55

If someone without a leader badge asks for a health task, you kindly say 'that has to come from the doctor or nurse.'

### Question 56

Health tasks come from the doctor, while the manager handles schedules and supplies.

### Question 57

Whether the PA can be in charge is decided by the rules and the office's plan, not by age or friendship.

### Question 58

If a task seems like more than you are trained for, you speak up and check before doing it.

### Question 59

If you get an important note, you double-check it and write it down so nothing is forgotten.

### Question 60

A helper can fetch and assist, but cannot become the doctor.

### Question 61

Scope is the fence around what you are allowed and able to do - you stay inside the fence.

### Question 62

You can hand someone their test paper, but only the teacher can explain what the score means.

### Question 63

You follow a direction when it is safe, within your abilities, and clearly explained.

### Question 64

If you don't understand a note, you ask the writer before doing anything - never guess.

### Question 65

You only push back when a job is too big or unsafe for you, not on everyday helper jobs.

### Question 66

Giving medicine is a job only trained helpers do; if you are not trained, you say no and get the nurse.

### Question 67

You repeat the message back and write it down right away so nothing gets mixed up.

### Question 68

If you are rusty at something, you tell the coach you need a quick practice first instead of faking it.

### Question 69

The rulebook, the leader's license, your training, and the office's rules decide what you may do.

### Question 70

'When you have time' still means it needs doing - you add it to your list and do it in the right order.

### Question 71

You do what the teacher clearly asks, and you raise your hand when something is unclear.

### Question 72

If something looks off, you show it to the teacher right away instead of guessing or hiding it.

### Question 73

If a direction could hurt someone, you say no right away and get a grown-up - you don't do it first.

### Question 74

If a leader pushes you to break a rule, you calmly say no and tell the principal.

### Question 75

Escalation is taking a problem to a bigger leader when you cannot fix it yourself.

### Question 76

If you see a spill about to happen, you shout 'stop!' right away - you don't wait.

### Question 77

You get a leader involved when something is unsafe, too big for you, or stuck.

### Question 78

When someone is upset about their care, you tell the teacher in charge instead of arguing.

### Question 79

You tell your teacher first so the right person can fix it the right way.

### Question 80

If a teammate is being unsafe, you tell the coach so everyone stays safe.

### Question 81

If the first teacher can't help, you go to the principal - you don't just give up.

### Question 82

If you spill something, you tell the teacher so it can be cleaned up - you don't hide it.

### Question 83

Writing down a problem is like keeping a note so everyone remembers what happened and what was done.

### Question 84

If you don't know the answer, you say 'let me get the teacher' instead of making something up.

### Question 85

You tell the teacher first, and if nothing changes, you tell the principal - in that order.
